about: What each target venue's own pages say about generative-AI content in submissions. Every entry quotes or paraphrases a page that was opened on the date given; 'policy' is one of prohibits (the venue asks authors to confirm AI did not generate the content), disclose (allowed with a disclosure statement; authors take full responsibility), unchecked. Read by venue_policy.py. Add a venue only after opening its page.

venues.name: International Journal of Fluid Power (River Publishers)
venues.summary: Submission checklist: 'The submission has not been generated by AI tools and is the original work of the authors listed. AI tools may be used to improve grammar, but not to generate "original" content.' The journal's publication-ethics page, read the same day, says instead that AI used to generate any content 'must be declared on submission and mentioned clearly in the text'; the checklist box is the stricter of the two and authors must tick it.

venues.name: ASME journals
venues.summary: AI Position Statement: 'ASME prohibits the use of generative AI in the creation of content for journal submissions. Authors are required to confirm that AI was not used in the development of their original work.' The page covers ASME journals; an ASME-co-sponsored conference (e.g. the Bath/ASME symposium) may follow it, not checked.

venues.name: IEEE publications (journals and letters, e.g. RA-L, Transactions on Power Systems)
venues.summary: Submission and peer-review policies: content generated by AI (text, figures, images, code) 'shall be disclosed in the acknowledgments section', naming the system and the sections that use it, with the level of use; editing and grammar use is recommended but not required to be disclosed.

venues.name: Elsevier journals (e.g. Automation in Construction, J. Power Sources, Ocean Engineering, Water Research)
venues.summary: Generative AI policies for journals: AI tools may support manuscript preparation but 'must never be used as a substitute for human critical thinking, expertise and evaluation'; the manuscript must reflect 'the author's own analysis, interpretation, insights and ideas', and a separate AI declaration statement is required on submission. Allowed only with real human oversight of the analysis, which an agent-run programme has to be able to show.

venues.name: arXiv (preprints)
venues.summary: Moderation policy: significant use of text-to-text generative AI is to be reported like other tools; every signing author takes full responsibility for all contents however generated; AI tools are not listed as authors.

venues.name: ASCE journals
venues.summary: ascelibrary.org returned 403 through the session proxy on 2026-11-19; policy not read.

venues.name: NeurIPS (conference)
venues.summary: NeurIPS 2025 LLM policy for authors: 'We welcome authors to use any tool that is suitable for preparing high-quality papers and research'; LLM use 'should be described in the experimental setup section (or equivalent) if it is an important, original, or non-standard component of the approach'; 'authors are responsible for the entire content of the paper, including all text, figures, and references'. Unverified LLM-generated references are named as a violation. The 2026 page was not checked.

venues.name: ICML (conference)
venues.summary: ICML 2026 call for papers, 'Generative AI Considerations': 'Authors are allowed to use generative AI tools such as Large Language Models (LLMs) to assist in writing or research. However, authors must take full responsibility for all content in their paper'; notable uses are encouraged, not required, to be explained; 'LLMs are not eligible for authorship'; prompt injection aimed at LLM reviewers means desk rejection.

venues.name: CoRL (Conference on Robot Learning)
venues.summary: Instructions for authors, 'Generative AI policies': papers citing references that do not exist are desk-rejected; 'Authors must take full responsibility for the content'; generative AI does not qualify for authorship; 'authors will be asked to briefly disclose how generative AI tools were used for research and paper writing'. References are checked with GPTZero.

venues.name: RSS (Robotics: Science and Systems)
venues.summary: Call for papers, 'Use of AI-Generated Text': 'The use of LLMs is permitted for both authors and reviewers. While disclosure is not mandatory, it is highly encouraged'; hallucinated citations mean desk rejection (checked automatically); authors are completely responsible for the content. A two-stage submission is meant 'to preserve human involvement and oversight'.

venues.name: Springer Nature journals (Springer, Nature Portfolio, BMC, Palgrave; e.g. Int. J. Philosophy of Religion)
match: International Journal for Philosophy of Religion
venues.summary: 'AI use in manuscript preparation', a three-level risk framework. Red, 'not permitted': 'AI replaces authorship or generates scholarly content without oversight', listing 'writing results or discussion independently; generating scientific claims or interpretations'. Amber (allowed, labelled): outlines and 'drafting sections based on author input'. 'AI can assist with expression, but the argument, interpretation, and conclusions must be author-led.' An agent-written results and discussion falls in red.

venues.name: Taylor & Francis journals
venues.summary: 'Using AI in your research and manuscript preparations', table of permitted uses: drafting manuscript text, 'No - Taylor & Francis does not allow generative AI to create a first draft of a manuscript or sections of a manuscript'; copyediting yes, but AI 'cannot be used to create or conclude the argument of an article'. AI in research methodology and data analysis is allowed with full records, including prompts.

venues.name: Wiley journals (e.g. Journal for the Scientific Study of Religion)
venues.summary: Best practice guidelines, 'Artificial Intelligence': authors 'may only use AI Technology as an additional tool in their writing process, not a replacement for their own expertise and judgement'; AI-generated content must be reviewed 'to ensure the final work reflects their own expertise, voice, and originality'; all AI use is documented and disclosed at submission, including 'whether it influenced key arguments or conclusions'. The fuller AI-guidelines page returned 403.

venues.name: Cambridge University Press journals (e.g. Religious Studies, Network Science)
venues.summary: Authorship and contributorship, 'AI Contributions to Research Content': 'AI use must be declared and clearly explained in publications such as research papers, just as we expect scholars to do with other software, tools and methodologies'; AI cannot be an author; authors are accountable for accuracy, integrity and originality; individual journals may set stricter rules (not checked per journal).
